title: Diachronic Drift
welcome_lead: From Old to Modern English, examine how phonology, lexis and grammar slip their moorings across the centuries.

concepts.def: Change observed across time, contrasted with synchronic snapshots of a single moment.
A systematic change in long vowel pronunciation in English roughly 1400-1700, reshaping the phonology.
Adoption of words from other languages: French (after 1066), Latin (Renaissance), global English borrowings.
The process by which lexical items become grammatical markers (Old English 'gan' to modern 'going to' future).
Semantic shift where a word acquires more positive connotations (knight: boy to noble warrior).
Semantic shift where a word acquires more negative connotations (silly: blessed to foolish).

walkthroughs.body_html:
Between roughly 1400 and 1700, English long vowels migrated upward and forward in the mouth. Bite, once /biːtə/, became /baɪt/.

This shift explains many of the mismatches between spelling and modern pronunciation — spelling was largely fixed before the shift completed.

After 1066 French became the language of court, leaving English a Germanic substrate with thousands of Romance borrowings (government, justice, beef).

Latin returned in the Renaissance as the lexicon of science and learning; later, global contact added bungalow, tsunami, emoji.

Grammaticalisation tracks how content words bleach into grammatical markers. Going began as motion verb plus purposive — I am going to London to study — and became a future auxiliary, I'm gonna study.

The process illustrates that grammar itself is the residue of past meaning.
